lessons.title: Lesson 1: Moving from doer to manager
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Describe how your job changes when you start managing people, and choose what to stop doing yourself.
This lesson builds toward: When you start managing people, you will describe how your job changes and choose one task to stop doing yourself, naming at least two parts of a manager's main job.
Many managers get the job because they were good at the work. But the job is now different: your results are the team's results. If you keep doing everything yourself, the team stops growing and you burn out.
Your new work is to make the goal clear, give people what they need, remove things that block them, help them improve, and notice good work. You still pitch in when it truly helps, but it is no longer your main job.
It is normal for this to feel strange, especially if you now manage former teammates. Be friendly, be fair to everyone, and be honest that your role has changed. Ask your own manager what success looks like for you.
Step by step:
- Write down the tasks you still do yourself every week.
- Mark the ones someone on the team could learn to do.
- Pick one to hand off this month.
- Ask your manager: "What would make my team a success in six months?"
Words to know:
- Manager: a person who is responsible for the results of a group of people, not only their own work.
- Direct report: a person whose manager you are.
Try it now: List five tasks you do every week. Circle one that someone on your team could learn. Write one sentence about who could take it and why it would help them.
You can now explain how a manager's job differs from a doer's job and pick one task to stop doing yourself.

check.q: Which is part of a manager's new work?
options: Doing every hard task personally
Making the goal clear and noticing good work
Avoiding former teammates
Checking every email the team sends
check.why: The manager's job is to make the goal clear, remove blockers, help people improve and notice good work.

check.q: You are new to managing and unsure what success looks like for you. What would you do?
options: Guess and hope for the best
Copy the last manager exactly
Ask the team to decide
Ask your own manager what success looks like
check.why: The lesson says to ask your own manager what success looks like.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting clear expectations and delegating
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a clear expectation and hand off a task with an outcome, a deadline and a check-in.
This lesson builds toward: Given one task for a team member, you will write a clear expectation and a delegation with the outcome, deadline, what they can decide and a check-in, so the person can say the task back in their own words.
Most team problems start with unclear expectations. People cannot hit a target they cannot see. A clear expectation says what the result is, how good it needs to be, and by when. "Keep the store clean" is vague. "Restock and face the front shelves by 9 am every day" is clear.
Delegating means handing someone a task and the authority to do it, not just the chores. Say what result you want and why it matters, the deadline, what they can decide on their own, and when you will check in. Then let them do it their way.
Match the handoff to the person. Someone new needs more steps and more check-ins. Someone experienced may only need the goal. Ask them to say back what they heard, so you both know you agree.
Step by step:
- Name the result you want and why it matters.
- Say how good it needs to be and the deadline.
- Say what they can decide alone and when to ask you.
- Agree a check-in time.
- Ask them to say back the task in their own words.
Words to know:
- Expectation: a clear statement of the result someone is responsible for and how it will be judged.
- Delegate: to give someone a task and the authority to do it.
- Check-in: a short planned talk to see how a task is going.
Try it now: Take the task you circled in Lesson 1. Write the handoff with all five parts. Read it to a friend or say it out loud, then ask yourself: could someone do this without asking me ten questions?
You can now write a clear expectation and delegate a task with a result, a deadline, decision limits and a check-in.

check.q: What three things does a clear expectation say?
options: The result, how good it needs to be, and by when
Who is in charge, the team name and the location
The pay, the hours and the breaks
The rules, the penalties and the forms
check.why: A clear expectation names the result, the quality and the deadline.

check.q: You hand a task to an experienced team member. What would you do?
options: Give every step and check in hourly
Give no deadline
Give the goal and deadline, then let them do it their way
Do half of it first
check.why: Match the handoff to the person; experienced people may only need the goal.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Running useful one-on-ones
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and hold a regular one-on-one that belongs to the team member.
This lesson builds toward: For one team member, you will plan a one-on-one agenda that starts with what is on their mind, covering progress, blockers and growth.
A one-on-one is a short, regular private meeting between you and one person on your team, often 20 to 30 minutes every week or two. It is the best place to catch problems early, build trust and help people grow.
Make it their meeting. Start with what is on their mind. Then talk about progress on their work, anything blocking them, and their growth. Save status updates you could read in a message for the message.
Protect the time: do not cancel often, put your phone away, and listen more than you talk. Write down any promise you make and keep it. Keep notes private and respectful.
Step by step:
- Book a regular time and keep it.
- Open with: "What's on your mind?"
- Ask about progress and what is blocking them.
- Talk about growth: "What do you want to get better at?"
- End by agreeing next steps, and write them down.
Words to know:
- One-on-one: a regular private meeting between a manager and one team member.
- Blocker: anything that stops someone from getting their work done.
Try it now: Write a one-on-one agenda for a real or pretend team member with four questions: one opener, one about progress, one about blockers, and one about growth.
You can now plan and hold a one-on-one that puts the team member's needs first and ends with clear next steps.

options: A yearly review
A short, regular private meeting with one team member
A team-wide meeting
A disciplinary hearing
check.why: One-on-ones are often 20 to 30 minutes every week or two.

check.q: Your one-on-ones keep turning into status updates. What would you change?
options: Cancel them
Make them longer
Hold them as a group
Move status to a message and start with what is on their mind
check.why: Make it their meeting; status you could read belongs in a message.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Feedback, performance and the team

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Giving feedback with situation-behavior-impact
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give specific feedback, positive or corrective, using situation-behavior-impact.
This lesson builds toward: Given something a team member did, you will write feedback in situation-behavior-impact form and ask how they see it, naming a specific behavior you saw or heard, with no "always" or "never".
Feedback works when it is specific, timely and about what someone did, not who they are. A simple way to say it is situation-behavior-impact, often called SBI.
Situation: when and where. Behavior: what the person did that you saw or heard. Impact: what happened because of it. For example: "In this morning's customer call (situation), you cut the customer off twice (behavior). She got upset and asked for a supervisor (impact)." Then ask: "How did you see it?" and agree a next step together.
Use SBI for praise too: "At Saturday's food drive, you set up the sign-in table early. We checked in 40 volunteers with no line." Give feedback soon, in private for corrections, and avoid words like "always" and "never".
Step by step:
- Situation: say when and where.
- Behavior: describe what they did, like a video camera would see it.
- Impact: say what happened because of it.
- Ask how they see it and listen.
- Agree a next step.
Words to know:
- Feedback: information about how someone's actions affected the work, given so they can keep doing it or change it.
- SBI: situation-behavior-impact: a way to give feedback that names when, what they did, and what happened.
Try it now: Write two SBI statements about real moments you saw: one to praise good work and one to fix a problem. Check that the behavior part describes only what you saw or heard.
You can now give specific, fair feedback with situation, behavior and impact, and turn it into a next step.

check.q: In SBI feedback, what is the "impact"?
options: What happened because of what the person did
When and where it happened
What you think of the person
The penalty for next time
check.why: Impact is the result of the behavior.

check.q: A team member stayed late to fix a customer's order. What would you say?
options: "You're always great."
"Thanks, I guess."
"Last night you fixed Ms. Lee's order, so she got it on time and thanked us."
Nothing; it is their job
check.why: SBI works for praise too: situation, behavior and impact.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Handling under-performance fairly
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Take a performance problem through clear, fair, written steps.
This lesson builds toward: Given a performance problem, you will plan a private talk and a written improvement plan, checking expectations first and including what good looks like, the support you will give and a review date.
When someone is not meeting expectations, act early. Waiting usually makes it worse and is unfair to the rest of the team. First check yourself: was the expectation clear? Did they have the training, tools and time?
Talk privately. Use SBI to name the gap, then ask what is getting in the way. Sometimes there is a cause you did not know about, like a health or family issue, a broken tool or confusing instructions. Agree a plan together: what good looks like, what support you will give, and a date to review.
Write down what you agreed, and follow up on that date. Treat everyone by the same standard. If things do not improve, or before any formal warning or firing, follow your organization's policy and talk to human resources or your own manager. Rules differ by place, so get advice when in doubt.
Step by step:
- Check: was the expectation clear, and did they have what they needed?
- Meet privately and name the gap with SBI.
- Ask what is getting in the way, and listen.
- Agree what good looks like, your support and a review date.
- Write it down and follow up on the date.
- Before formal steps, follow your policy and talk to HR or your manager.
Words to know:
- Under-performance: when someone's work is not meeting the expectations that were set.
- Improvement plan: a written agreement on what must change, the support given, and a date to review.
- HR: human resources: the people who handle hiring, policies and employee matters.
Try it now: Think of a real or made-up performance problem. Write the improvement plan in four lines: the gap (in SBI form), what good looks like, the support you will give, and the review date.
You can now handle a performance problem early and fairly with a private talk, a written plan and a follow-up.

check.q: What should you check before raising a performance problem?
options: Whether the expectation was clear and they had what they needed
Whether others also dislike them
Whether you can fire them today
Whether HR is busy
check.why: First check yourself: clear expectations, training, tools and time.

check.q: You agreed an improvement plan with a review date. What would you do on that date?
options: Forget it if things seem fine
Follow up and write down what happened
Give a formal warning without talking
Start a new plan with a new person
check.why: Write down what you agreed and follow up on that date.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Team meetings and recognition
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a short team meeting that ends with clear actions and specific thanks.
This lesson builds toward: For a regular team meeting, you will write a short agenda that ends with actions and one specific thank-you, with who will do what by when, sent out the same day.
A good team meeting has a purpose, an agenda sent ahead, a start and end time, and a list of actions at the end. If you only need to share news, send a message instead.
Run it on time. Go around so quieter people speak, keep side topics for later, and end by reading back each action: who will do what, by when. Send the actions out the same day. An AI assistant can help you turn your notes into a clean list, but check it.
Recognition keeps people going. Thank people often, soon, and specifically, and say how their work helped. Some people like public praise; others prefer a private word or note. Ask them what they like.
Step by step:
- Write the purpose and a short agenda; send it ahead.
- Start and end on time.
- Invite every person to speak.
- Close by reading back actions: who, what, by when.
- Send the actions the same day.
- Give one specific thank-you.
Words to know:
- Agenda: the list of topics for a meeting, in order.
- Action item: a task agreed in a meeting, with a person and a deadline.
- Recognition: showing people you noticed and value their work.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page "first 30 days" plan. Include expectations for one role, one task to delegate, a one-on-one agenda, one SBI feedback note, and a 20-minute meeting agenda that ends with actions and one specific thank-you.
You can now run a short, focused team meeting, close it with clear actions, and recognize good work in a way people value.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear expectations The expectation is vague, such as "keep things tidy". Says the result, how good it needs to be, and by when. Also says why the result matters. Delegated task The task has no deadline or check-in. States the outcome, deadline, what the person can decide and a check-in. Fits the handoff to the person's experience. One-on-one agenda The agenda is only status updates. Starts with what is on their mind and covers progress, blockers and growth. Includes a way to track promises you make. SBI feedback The feedback is about the person, or uses "always" or "never". Names the situation, a specific behavior and its impact. Ends with a question that invites their view and a next step. Team meeting and thanks No actions at the end, or the thanks is general. A 20-minute agenda that ends with who will do what by when, and one specific thank-you. Gives quieter people a turn and plans to send actions the same day. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a good team meeting have?
options: No agenda so it stays flexible
A purpose, an agenda sent ahead, start and end times and actions
Only the manager speaking
No set end time
check.why: These parts keep a meeting short and useful.

check.q: A quiet team member likes private thanks. What would you do?
options: Praise them loudly in the meeting anyway
Skip thanking them
Thank them in the team chat
Give them a specific thank-you in a private word or note
check.why: Ask people what recognition they like and respect it.
